note.text: A conditional links antecedent to consequent without asserting either separately. Material implication is false only for true P and false Q. Preserve direction, distinguish necessary from sufficient, and do not confuse a truth function with causal evidence.

sections.heading: Your goal and connections
sections.text: By the end, you should be able to identify antecedent and consequent, preserve the direction of a condition and recognise its counterexample. Builds on: a proposition as a truth-valued claim; categorical inclusion as a directed relation. Leads to: disjunctions and the later symbolic-logic truth tables.

sections.heading: A compound with a direction
sections.text: If P then Q is a conditional: P is the antecedent and Q the consequent. Under the stated rule, P is sufficient for Q and Q necessary for P. The rule does not assert P, and it does not automatically reverse. If a fictional club meets, then its room is reserved does not say a reserved room guarantees a club meeting.

sections.heading: Find the violating case
sections.text: For the material-conditional convention, the conditional is false only when P is true and Q false. True/true, false/true and false/false do not refute it. A false antecedent does not establish that a real causal explanation is good: truth-functional evaluation and causal evidence are different questions. These exercises state their convention explicitly.

sections.heading: Use the relation carefully
sections.text: A club meeting without the required reservation refutes the invented rule. A reservation without a meeting need not refute it: another group could have booked the room. Do not infer P from Q alone. When translating only if, the condition following only if is necessary: P only if Q becomes If P then Q.

key_words.meaning: one that guarantees the consequent under the stated rule
a case fulfilling P without Q

mistake.wrong: If P then Q permits inferring P just from Q.
mistake.right: The direction is from P to Q; the converse needs support.
mistake.why: Q can be true for another reason.

worked_example.problem: A fictional rule says: If the club meets, the room is reserved. The room is reserved. Must the club meet?
steps: P is the meeting; Q is the reservation.
The rule forbids P without Q.
Q without P remains possible: another activity may use the reservation.
worked_example.answer: No. Inferring P from Q alone reverses the rule.

questions.prompt: Find the incorrect claim, then read the reason for the correction.

right.explain: This is a correct rule: The antecedent is the if-clause. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.
This is a correct rule: The consequent is the then-clause. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

right.text: A true P and false Q refute If P then Q.
right.explain: This is a correct rule: A true P and false Q refute If P then Q. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

right.text: A conditional does not by itself assert its antecedent.
right.explain: This is a correct rule: A conditional does not by itself assert its antecedent. Look for a claim that breaks a rule taught in Learn.

wrong.text: If P then Q always also asserts If Q then P.
wrong.explain: That converse needs separate support; P may not be the only sufficient condition for Q.

wrong.text: A false antecedent makes the material conditional false.
wrong.explain: Only true P with false Q makes the material conditional false.

wrong.text: Q alone establishes P whenever If P then Q is accepted.
wrong.explain: That affirms the consequent; Q may hold for another reason.

wrong.text: A formal conditional necessarily establishes a real causal connection.
wrong.explain: A truth-functional relation is not by itself evidence of causation.
